description: CLPS Challenge with potential to switch to pick moon base locations
summary:
We chose the lunar landing challenge, with the goal of making lunar data available to the average person. Our goal was to develop a tool that could be used by anybody to explore and compare different places on the moon for landing sites or research expeditions. To do this, we developed Lunar Listings, a website that determines the viability of different plots on the moon and presents them as real-estate listings for a user to browse.
Each real-estate listing takes into account what % of the year the property is in the sun, the % of the year communication with earth is viable, and how safe a landing site is based on topography maps. Through an easy to use UI, Lunar Listings allows anybody to explore what kinds of terrain and resources are available on the moon and plan their own lunar missions and futures; getting the average person interested in the moon.
details:
Lunar Listings is a Zillow-style real-estate site for the Moon. The premise is fictional, but every price and score comes from real NASA data. It was built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Lunar Landing Site Navigator).

What it does and how it works

Users browse a map of lunar "plots" the way they would browse homes on Zillow. Each plot has a listing page, filters, sorting, map overlays and a price called the Moonstimate.

- Two tiers of plots.
- Moon-wide: 64,800 plots (1° × 1°), scored for Sun and Earth visibility over 2028, slope and roughness, temperature and nearby landmarks.
- South Pole District: 78,464 plots (960 m each, inside 85°S) on 240 m terrain cells. This tier adds terrain-aware light and Earth contact using horizon profiles every 2°, permanently shadowed regions, distance to ice, and a 3D Tour.
- Data pipeline (Python). It turns raw NASA data into static files. It computes ephemerides with JPL Horizons and uses LOLA and PGDA terrain for landing safety. It models sunlight and solar power from terrain horizons, and takes temperatures from LRO Diviner. Earth contact requires the Earth to be at least 1° above local terrain. IAU place names supply landmarks.
- Scoring and pricing. Four scored systems feed a viability score and then a price: landing safety, sunlight and power, temperature, and Earth communication. The price uses a $5,000 base and a steepness constant k of 6.9. Every weight and threshold lives in config/*.yaml.
- Web app (React + deck.gl). It loads the pre-generated data and has no backend. It mirrors the same formulas in TypeScript, and the two implementations are checked against shared golden vectors.

Benefits

- It makes site-selection science (illumination, slope, thermal environment, communication) approachable for non-experts.
- Plots can be compared at a glance with familiar tools such as filters, sort and overlays.
- It works without a server. The generated data is committed, so it is easy to host and reproduce.
- Assumptions are explicit and tunable, and make validate cross-checks results against NASA data.

Intended impact

- Get people, especially students and the public, interested in lunar exploration and the Artemis South Pole region.
- Show why landing sites differ: some are lit nearly all year, some sit in permanent shadow, and Earth visibility varies.
- Serve as a template for turning open planetary datasets into an interactive decision tool.

Tools, languages and software

- Languages and frameworks: Python 3.11, NumPy and Numba for the pipeline. TypeScript, React 18, deck.gl 9, Zustand, Recharts and react-window for the app.
- Build and test: Vite, Vitest, Playwright, pytest, ESLint, uv, Make, and GitHub Actions deploying to GitHub Pages.
- Data: JPL Horizons, LOLA and PGDA terrain and illumination products, LRO Diviner thermal data, USGS/IAU nomenclature, and NASA Trek and LROC QuickMap for reference.
- Hardware: standard laptops. The raw download is about 15 GB, but the rebuild takes about 30 seconds from the cached data.
- Development process: two Claude Code agents built the project in parallel, a Pipeline agent and an App agent. They coordinated through single-writer logs and a versioned data contract in docs/agents/, with humans making the decisions.

Creativity

- Framing serious mission-planning science as a real-estate marketplace, with a Moonstimate, home types and a Buy/Rent toggle (built but switched off), makes the data approachable and memorable.
- The 3D Tour and the scenario demos, such as the "Shackleton ridge" plot, add storytelling on top of the numbers.
- The two-tier design shows the whole Moon but goes deep on the South Pole.

Factors the team considered

- Scientific honesty: the premise is fictional but the data is real, and prices are labelled as model outputs. The About dialog and docs/validation.md list the assumptions.
- Terrain-aware modelling: the Sun and Earth are judged against local horizons, not a flat Moon.
- Performance and size: it is a static site of about 160 MB, mostly data, with budgets on build time and load.
- Consistency: the frozen data contract and the Python-to-TypeScript parity tests keep the two halves in agreement.
- Reproducibility and maintainability: config-driven tunables, committed generated data, and CI lint, type-check and tests.
